anchor: a great tripod and a cauldron
title: The Phaeacians' parting gifts
greek: τρίποδα μέγαν ἠδὲ λέβητα (tripoda megan ēde lebēta), 'a great tripod and a cauldron'; προικός (proikos), 'as a free gift'
short: Alcinous asks each Phaeacian lord to add a tripod and cauldron to Odysseus' gifts, recovering the cost from the people.
body: The gifts already promised in Book 8 (8.387-445) were clothing and gold; now each lord adds bronze vessels, the classic prestige objects of the heroic world, valued for their metal and displayed as signs of status and friendship. Alcinous' explanation is frankly economic: 'we will repay ourselves' (tisometha) by a levy on the people, since it would be hard for one man to give 'as a free gift' (proikos, Monro: 'without such repayment', Latin gratis). The gifts matter for the plot. Poseidon later complains that Odysseus now has more than his share of Trojan spoil would have been (13.135-8), so the man who lost everything at sea comes home richer than he left. Between 1930 and 1932 Sylvia Benton excavated the cave at Polis Bay on Ithaca and found the remains of about twelve bronze tripod-cauldrons of the ninth and eighth centuries BC; she suggested they were offerings to Odysseus, but the identification of that cave with anything in Homer remains disputed.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.13-15.
Homer, Odyssey 13.10-15.
Homer, Odyssey 8.387-395 (the first round of gifts).

anchor: as a man longs for supper
title: Simile of the ploughman at sunset
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτ' ἀνὴρ δόρποιο λιλαίεται (hōs d' hot' anēr dorpoio lilaietai), 'as when a man longs for supper'
short: Odysseus watches the sun go down like a ploughman who has worked all day and longs for his supper.
body: At the Phaeacian feast Odysseus keeps turning to the sun, wanting it to set so that he can sail. Homer compares him not to a warrior or a sailor but to a farmer whose pair of oxen has dragged the plough through fallow land all day: the end of the light is welcome because it brings food and rest. The comparison quietly moves Odysseus out of the fairy-tale world of Phaeacia into the working world of Ithaca, where he will soon live among herdsmen and later boast of his skill at ploughing (18.366-75). Monro notes that the plough's epithet pēkton, 'put together', marks it as a jointed piece of craftsmanship, and that the phrase dunai epeigomenos (13.30) means 'eager for its setting'. The weary knees of the ploughman also anticipate the exhausted traveller who will sleep through the whole voyage.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.30 and 13.32.

title: Odysseus' death-like sleep
greek: νήγρετος, ἥδιστος, θανάτῳ ἄγχιστα ἐοικώς (nēgretos, hēdistos, thanatōi anchista eoikōs)
short: Odysseus crosses from Phaeacia to Ithaca in an 'unwaking' sleep 'most like to death', a passage between two worlds.
body: LSJ glosses nēgretos (from ne- 'not' and egeirō 'wake') as 'unwaking', 'sound'. The sleep is a gift but also a kind of death: Odysseus leaves the half-magical world of Phaeacia and is reborn on his own shore, not knowing where he is. Sleep has been dangerous for him before: he slept as Ithaca came into sight and his men opened the bag of winds (10.31-55), and he slept on Thrinacia while they killed the Sun's cattle (12.338-73). This time the sleep is safe and the crew are kind. Greek poetry made Sleep and Death twin brothers (Hesiod, Theogony 211-12 and 756-66; Il. 16.672, where they carry Sarpedon home), so the comparison is traditional, but here it gives the homecoming the shape of a return from the dead. Monro, noting the metre, wonders whether hēdistos 'sweetest' has displaced an older word.

title: The Phaeacian ship like a chariot team
greek: τετράοροι ἄρσενες ἵπποι (tetraoroi arsenes hippoi); ἴρηξ κίρκος (irēx kirkos), 'the circling hawk'
short: The ship leaps forward like a four-horse chariot under the lash, faster than the swiftest hawk.
body: Two images measure the speed of the magic ship. First, a team of four stallions on a plain, rearing up together under the whip: the stern (prumnē) rises as the ship surges, and Monro defends this reading against those who would change it to 'prow' for realism. Second, not even the kirkos, 'swiftest of winged things', could keep pace. Monro explains that in the pair irēx kirkos the first word is generic ('hawk') and the second specific, as in 'ox bull', and LSJ adds that the species cannot be identified. Phaeacian ships are elsewhere 'swift as a wing or a thought' (7.36) and need no helmsman (8.557-63); the similes keep that marvel in view on the last voyage they will ever make, since Poseidon turns this ship to stone on its return.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.81, 13.84 and 13.86.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. κίρκος.

anchor: peer of the gods in counsel
title: An echo of the proem
greek: ὃς πρὶν μὲν μάλα πολλὰ πάθ' ἄλγεα ὃν κατὰ θυμόν (hos prin men mala polla path' algea hon kata thumon)
short: The poet sums up Odysseus in words that recall the opening lines of the poem, marking the end of the wanderings.
body: The ship carries 'a man the peer of the gods in counsel, who in time past had suffered many griefs at heart'. The phrase pathen algea hon kata thumon repeats Od. 1.4, and the double list of 'wars of men and grievous waves' sums up the Iliad's war and the Odyssey's sea. Now he 'slept in peace, forgetful of all that he had suffered'. Many readers therefore treat the landing on Ithaca as the hinge of the poem: the first half (wanderings, told largely by Odysseus himself) closes, and the second (revenge at home) begins. Monro notes that theois enalinkia mēdea is a compressed comparison ('counsels like those of the gods'), and that 'passing through' (peirōn) strictly fits only the waves, not the wars. The contrast between past suffering and present oblivion makes the sleeping hero vulnerable, which the next scenes exploit.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.89 and 13.91.
Homer, Odyssey 1.1-5 (the proem).
Homer, Odyssey 13.89-92.

title: The morning star
greek: ἀστὴρ ... φαάντατος, ὅς τε μάλιστα ἔρχεται ἀγγέλλων φάος Ἠοῦς (astēr ... phaantatos)
short: The planet Venus as morning star, which 'comes to herald the light of Dawn', marks the moment of arrival in Ithaca.
body: Homer does not name the star, but it is the one the Iliad calls Heōsphoros, 'Light-bringer', which 'goes to announce light upon the earth' (Il. 23.226): the planet Venus seen before sunrise. The arrival at the very moment of dawn is symbolic, since a new day and a new phase of the story begin together. Monro uses the line to keep the poem's careful timetable: this is the dawn of the 35th day of the action, counting from the council of the gods in Book 1. Time-markers of this kind are frequent in Books 13-16, where two plots (Odysseus in the swineherd's hut, Telemachus returning from Sparta) must be kept in step.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 13.93.

title: The harbour of Phorcys
greek: Φόρκυνος ... λιμήν, ἁλίοιο γέροντος (Phorkunos ... limēn, halioio gerontos)
short: A sheltered harbour on Ithaca named after Phorcys, an 'old man of the sea' and grandfather of the Cyclops Polyphemus.
body: Phorcys is one of the old sea-gods, son of Pontus and Earth in Hesiod (Theogony 237) and father of many monsters. The Odyssey has already named him as father of the nymph Thoosa, mother of Polyphemus by Poseidon (1.71-3), so Odysseus is set down in a bay belonging to the grandfather of the Cyclops whose blinding caused all his troubles. The harbour is a perfect natural shelter: two headlands 'crouch towards' the entrance (Monro on potipeptēuiai), keeping out the swell, so that ships within need no cable once they reach 'the measure of anchorage' (hormou metron). Visitors since antiquity have tried to locate it: the bay of Dexia near Vathy is the traditional candidate, while others, impressed by the finds in the cave at Polis Bay, look to the north of the island.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.98, 13.99 and 13.101.
Hesiod, Theogony 237, 270-336 (Phorcys and his offspring).

title: The cave of the Naiad nymphs
greek: ἄντρον ἐπήρατον ἠεροειδές, ἱρὸν νυμφάων αἳ νηϊάδες καλέονται (antron epēraton ēeroeides, hiron numphaōn hai nēiades kaleontai)
short: A cave sacred to the water-nymphs, with stone bowls, looms and two doors, one for men and one for the gods.
body: Naiads are nymphs of springs and running water. Their cave has stone mixing-bowls and jars where bees store honey, long stone looms on which the nymphs weave sea-purple cloth (probably the poet's view of stalactites), ever-flowing springs, and two entrances: a northern one for mortals and a southern one, 'more divine' (theōterai, which Monro takes as 'divine' in contrast to the human door), which is the path of the immortals. In the third century AD the Neoplatonist Porphyry wrote a whole treatise, On the Cave of the Nymphs, reading it as an image of the cosmos, with the northern gate as the descent of souls into birth and the southern as their ascent. On Ithaca itself, the cave at Polis Bay excavated by Sylvia Benton yielded Geometric bronze tripods and a late terracotta mask inscribed with a vow to Odysseus, though later scholars doubt that it was the poet's cave. Odysseus will hide his treasure here (13.366-71).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.108 and 13.111.
Porphyry, On the Cave of the Nymphs, chs. 9-11 (trans. Thomas Taylor, 1823).

title: Poseidon's honour (timē)
greek: οὐκέτ' ἐγώ γε μετ' ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι τιμήεις ἔσομαι, ὅτε με βροτοὶ οὔ τι τίουσιν (timēeis esomai, hote me brotoi ou ti tiousin)
short: Poseidon complains that he will lose honour among the gods if mortals, even his own Phaeacians, ignore him.
body: Divine honour (timē) in Homer is partly a matter of recognition by mortals: a god whose wishes are ignored loses standing among the other gods. Poseidon's grievance is sharpened because the Phaeacians are 'of my own lineage' (13.130; their founder Nausithous was Poseidon's son, 7.56-62). Zeus reassures him that the gods do not dishonour their 'eldest and best', but adds that a mortal who fails to honour him may be punished. Monro points out the play between tiei, 'pays honour', and tisis, 'payment' in the sense of vengeance (13.144): honour withheld is repaid with punishment. The exchange shows the gods' politics in miniature. Zeus does not stop Poseidon; he steers him towards a punishment that is spectacular rather than total (see the petrified ship).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.142-144.
Homer, Odyssey 7.56-62 (the Phaeacians' descent from Poseidon).
Homer, Odyssey 13.128-145.

title: The Phaeacian ship turned to stone
greek: θεῖναι λίθον ἐγγύθι γαίης νηῒ θοῇ ἴκελον (theinai lithon engguthi gaiēs nēi thoēi ikelon); μέγα δέ σφιν ὄρος πόλει ἀμφικαλύψαι
short: Poseidon petrifies the returning ship in sight of the city, fulfilling an old prophecy; whether he also buries the city is left open.
body: Alcinous recognises the fulfilment of his father Nausithous' prophecy (already told at 8.564-71): Poseidon would strike a Phaeacian ship returning from a convoy and 'fling a great mountain about' the city. The Phaeacians at once abandon their tradition of carrying strangers home and sacrifice twelve bulls; the poem leaves them praying at the altar and never returns to them. Zeus' words at 13.158 were disputed in antiquity: Aristophanes of Byzantium read mēde ('and do not hide their city'), making Zeus forbid the mountain, but Monro keeps the transmitted text and argues that the elders' later prayers need not affect what Zeus says. The story is aetiological, explaining a ship-shaped rock; Monro notes that an islet near the old harbour of Corfu (ancient Corcyra, often identified with Scheria) was pointed out as the ship, citing Pliny, Natural History 4.53.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.154-158 and 13.158.
Homer, Odyssey 8.564-571 (Nausithous' prophecy).
Homer, Odyssey 13.172-187.

anchor: the goddess had shed a mist
title: Athena's mist over Ithaca
greek: περὶ γὰρ θεὸς ἠέρα χεῦε Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη (peri gar theos ēera cheue Pallas Athēnaiē)
short: Athena hides Ithaca from Odysseus in a mist so that she can disguise him and plan with him before anyone recognises him.
body: Odysseus wakes in his own country and does not know it. The mist does not make him invisible; as Monro explains, it gives Athena time to consult with him and change his appearance (done at 13.429-38), so that he does not rush straight to his palace and ruin everything. The poet states the purpose before the action ('that she might render him unknown, and tell him all things'), an order Monro calls prothysteron, putting the more definite act first. Athena has used a mist before to protect him as he entered the Phaeacian city (7.14-17, 7.140-3). The device also creates one of the poem's great ironies: the man who longed for Ithaca for twenty years laments that he has been abandoned in a strange land, smiting his thighs in grief, while standing on his own shore.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.190 and 13.191.
Homer, Odyssey 7.14-17 (Athena's mist in Phaeacia).
Homer, Odyssey 13.187-196.

title: Zeus Hiketesios, protector of suppliants
greek: Ζεὺς ... ἱκετήσιος (Zeus ... hiketēsios)
short: Zeus as guardian of suppliants, invoked by Odysseus against the Phaeacians whom he wrongly thinks have cheated him.
body: Hiketēsios, from hiketēs, 'suppliant', names Zeus as the god who protects those who come with a plea and punishes anyone who wrongs them; LSJ cites this line for the title, which is equivalent to the later hikesios. The same Zeus appears in Odysseus' warning to the Cyclops as 'avenger of suppliants and strangers' (9.269-71). The curse is ironic twice over: the Phaeacians have been model hosts, and at this very moment they are being punished by Poseidon precisely for their hospitality. Monro records that Zenodotus read the imperative tisasthō ('let him punish'), and that some ancient critics probably thought a command addressed to a god improper. The line belongs to a cluster of cult titles in Books 13-16 (Zeus of strangers, of suppliants, of the hearth) that keep the ethics of hospitality in view as Odysseus moves among hosts good and bad.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἱκετήσιος.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), critical note on 13.213.
Homer, Odyssey 9.269-271 (Zeus avenger of suppliants and strangers).

title: Athena disguised as a young shepherd
greek: ἀνδρὶ δέμας εἰκυῖα νέῳ, ἐπιβώτορι μήλων, παναπάλῳ, οἷοί τε ἀνάκτων παῖδες ἔασι (andri demas eikuia neōi, epibōtori mēlōn)
short: Athena meets Odysseus disguised as a delicate young shepherd of princely look; the master of disguise is himself deceived.
body: The goddess comes as a young herdsman, 'most delicate, as are the sons of princes', with a fine cloak, sandals and a spear. The description closely resembles Hermes' disguise when he meets Priam as a young prince (Il. 24.347-8) and his appearance to Odysseus on Circe's island (10.277-9): gods often appear to mortals as attractive young men at moments of danger. Odysseus responds correctly by the rules of supplication, praying to the stranger 'as to a god' and coming 'to thy dear knees', and then tells his first false tale. The comedy of the scene lies in two masters of disguise each concealing their identity; only when Athena reveals herself (13.287-9, now as a tall and skilled woman) does Odysseus remark that the goddess takes 'what shape thou wilt' (13.312-13).

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 24.347-348 (Hermes as a young prince).
Homer, Odyssey 10.277-279 (Hermes meets Odysseus).
Homer, Odyssey 13.221-225.

title: Athena's description of Ithaca
greek: ἦ τοι μὲν τρηχεῖα καὶ οὐχ ἱππήλατός ἐστιν, οὐδὲ λίην λυπρή (trēcheia kai ouch hippēlatos)
short: Athena describes Ithaca as rocky and narrow but fertile, saving its name for the very end of her speech.
body: The goddess teases the stranger as a fool for not knowing so famous a land, then lists its qualities: rugged, unsuited to horses, narrow but not poor, rich in grain and wine, rain and dew, good for goats and cattle, with trees and springs. Telemachus had said much the same to Menelaus when refusing a gift of horses (4.601-8). The name itself is withheld until the last line, where it falls with emphasis: 'the name of Ithaca has reached even to Troy'. Monro notes that metopisthe at 13.241 means 'westwards', the west being the end of the day as the east is its beginning. Where Homer's Ithaca lay has been debated since antiquity, because the poem's description of it as 'furthest towards the west' (9.25-6) does not obviously fit modern Ithaki. Most scholars accept the traditional identification, while R. Bittlestone, J. Diggle and J. Underhill, Odysseus Unbound (Cambridge, 2005), argue for the Paliki peninsula of Cephalonia.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.238 and 13.241.
Homer, Odyssey 4.601-608 (Telemachus on Ithaca).
Homer, Odyssey 9.21-27 (Odysseus describes Ithaca).
R. Bittlestone, with J. Diggle and J. Underhill, Odysseus Unbound: The Search for Homer's Ithaca (Cambridge University Press, 2005).

title: The first 'Cretan' lie
greek: πυνθανόμην Ἰθάκης γε καὶ ἐν Κρήτῃ εὐρείῃ (punthanomēn Ithakēs ge kai en Krētēi eureiēi)
short: Odysseus invents a Cretan identity: an exile who killed Idomeneus' son Orsilochus and was abandoned on Ithaca by Phoenician sailors.
body: This is the first of the false autobiographies Odysseus tells in the second half of the poem (to Eumaeus in Book 14, to Penelope in Book 19, and in a different form to Laertes in Book 24). Each borrows from his real story (Trojan booty, a refusal to serve under another commander, sea-travel with strangers) and adapts it to the listener; the narrator later describes such tales as 'many lies like the truth' (19.203), a phrase close to the Muses' boast in Hesiod, Theogony 27. Crete was the obvious home for a liar: Epimenides' line 'Cretans are always liars' is quoted in Titus 1:12, and Callimachus applies it in his Hymn to Zeus (line 8). Monro paraphrases 13.254 'took back his speech' as leaving unsaid what he would have said if he had spoken the truth. The killer seeking refuge also prepares us for Theoclymenus (15.272-8) and for the slaughter to come.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.254-255.
Homer, Odyssey 19.203 ('many lies like the truth').
Titus 1:12 (King James Version).
Callimachus, Hymn 1 (To Zeus), line 8.

anchor: Cunning must he be and knavish
title: Athena and Odysseus: a partnership in cunning (mētis)
greek: κερδαλέος κ' εἴη καὶ ἐπίκλοπος (kerdaleos k' eiē kai epiklopos); ἐγὼ δ' ἐν πᾶσι θεοῖσι μήτι τε κλέομαι καὶ κέρδεσιν
short: Athena smiles at the lie, strokes Odysseus and praises him as best of mortals in cunning, as she is best among the gods.
body: This is one of the warmest scenes between a god and a mortal in Homer. Athena calls Odysseus 'bold' (schetlie, which Monro reads as friendly and admiring), 'crafty in counsel, insatiate in deceit', and claims kinship: he is first among mortals in counsel and speech, she is famed among the gods for mētis (practical intelligence) and kerdea (shrewd advantage-seeking). LSJ glosses mētis as 'wisdom, skill, craft'; Hesiod makes Athena the daughter of Metis, swallowed by Zeus (Theogony 886-900), so cunning is her birthright. Monro notes that kerdaleos means 'crafty' and that pedothen (13.295) probably means 'constantly' rather than 'from childhood'. The scene redefines heroism for the second half of the poem: Odysseus will win not by force alone but by disguise, patience and lies, under the protection of a goddess who enjoys his deceptions.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.291, 13.293 and 13.295.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. μῆτις.
Hesiod, Theogony 886-900 (Metis, mother of Athena).

anchor: never since then have I seen
title: Why was Athena absent?
greek: οὐ σέ γ' ἔπειτα ἴδον, κούρη Διός (ou se g' epeita idon, kourē Dios); πατροκασιγνήτῳ (patrokasignētōi), 'my father's brother'
short: Odysseus reproaches Athena for deserting him after Troy; she answers that she would not fight her uncle Poseidon.
body: Odysseus' complaint is just: Athena, his constant helper at Troy, never appeared during the adventures of Books 9-12. Her reply (13.339-43) is that she always knew he would come home, but did not wish to quarrel with Poseidon, her father's brother, angry over the blinding of his son. Many readers find the answer evasive. The poem elsewhere hints at a wider anger of Athena against the Greeks after the sack of Troy (Nestor at 3.130-5; Phemius' song of the 'woeful return' at 1.326-7), an idea developed by Jenny Strauss Clay in The Wrath of Athena (Princeton, 1983). Monro discusses 13.320-3, which are generally condemned as spurious: he finds 320-1 certainly interpolated, and for 322-3 notes the ancient objection that Odysseus could not know Athena had been present in Phaeacia, where she never revealed herself. He thinks the objection too literal but grants that the lines have the air of an insertion.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 13.320-323.
Homer, Odyssey 3.130-135 (Athena's anger after Troy).
Jenny Strauss Clay, The Wrath of Athena: Gods and Men in the Odyssey (Princeton University Press, 1983).

title: Odysseus recognises Ithaca
greek: σκέδασ' ἠέρα, εἴσατο δὲ χθών (skedas' ēera, eisato de chthōn); κύσε δὲ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν
short: Athena points out harbour, olive, cave and Mount Neriton, lifts the mist, and Odysseus kisses his native earth.
body: The recognition of the homeland is staged as a sequence of landmarks already described by the narrator: the harbour of Phorcys, the long-leaved olive at its head, the cave of the Naiads, and finally Mount Neriton, which Odysseus himself had named to the Phaeacians as the sign of Ithaca (9.21-2). Only then does the mist scatter. His response repeats a gesture: he kisses 'the earth, the giver of grain', as he did on reaching the Phaeacian shore (5.463). He then prays to the Naiads, whom he greets with the conventional chairete ('hail', though Monro notes the dative of prayers gives it some of its literal sense 'be glad'), and promises gifts 'as aforetime', which shows that he had worshipped at this cave before the war. The vow includes Telemachus, whom he hopes to see grow to manhood (13.358-60).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.347-348, 13.357 and 13.358.
Homer, Odyssey 9.21-22 (Neriton named).
Homer, Odyssey 5.463 (the first kiss of the earth).

title: Athena Ageleiē, 'driver of spoil'
greek: Διὸς θυγάτηρ ἀγελείη (Dios thugatēr ageleiē)
short: An old epithet of Athena as war-goddess, explained in antiquity as 'she who drives off the booty'.
body: LSJ explains ageleiē as equivalent to agousa leian, 'driving spoil', 'the forager', the goddess who carries off plunder (cattle and goods) in a raid; it is used in the Iliad (for example 6.269, 4.128). Some modern scholars prefer other derivations, so the meaning is not certain, but the ancient one fits Athena's role as patron of successful warfare. The epithet is pointed here: Odysseus prays that the goddess of victory will let him live and see his son grow up, a prayer that already looks forward to the battle with the suitors. It recurs when he names Athena as the author of his transformation (16.207), the only other place it appears in the Odyssey.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἀγελείη.
Homer, Iliad 6.269 (Athena ageleiē).
Homer, Odyssey 16.207 (the epithet repeated).

title: 'Loosing the diadem' of Troy
greek: Τροίης λύομεν λιπαρὰ κρήδεμνα (Troiēs luomen lipara krēdemna)
short: The walls of Troy pictured as a city's head-dress, 'loosed' when the city fell.
body: A krēdemnon is a woman's head-dress or veil (LSJ), worn by Andromache (Il. 22.470) and by Penelope when she appears before the suitors (Od. 1.334). In the plural it is used metaphorically of a city's battlements, which crown the walls; Akhilleus wishes that he and Patroclus alone might 'loose Troy's sacred diadem' (Il. 16.100). Monro calls the phrase a refinement of the commoner image in which a city's towers are its 'head'. The metaphor makes the sack of a city a kind of violation of a woman, as Andromache throwing off her head-dress at Hector's death (Il. 22.468-72) anticipates the fate of Troy itself. Odysseus recalls the occasion here to ask Athena for the same courage she gave him then; he claims he could fight three hundred men with her help.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 13.388.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. κρήδεμνον.

title: Odysseus transformed into an old beggar
greek: κάρψω μὲν χρόα καλόν (karpsō men chroa kalon); ξανθὰς δ' ἐκ κεφαλῆς ὀλέσω τρίχας (xanthas ... trichas, 'fair hair')
short: Athena withers Odysseus' skin, removes his fair hair, dims his eyes and gives him a beggar's rags, staff and wallet.
body: The disguise is announced and then carried out in almost the same words, a typical Homeric pattern. It is total: old skin, lost hair, bleared eyes, a filthy cloak and tunic, a hairless deer-skin, a staff and a battered beggar's wallet (pērē) on a twisted cord. Monro notes that here Odysseus has 'yellow' (xanthos) hair, whereas at 16.176 his restored beard is 'dark', a small inconsistency he compares with changes in a heroine's hair colour in Scott's Heart of Midlothian; on 13.400 he discusses how to construe 'such that a man would shudder to see'. The beggar's disguise lets Odysseus test the loyalty of everyone in Ithaca, and also lowers the king to the lowest social rank, from which he must rise again. It is reversed briefly for Telemachus (16.172-6) and finally after the slaughter (23.153-63).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 13.400, 13.431, 13.437 and 16.176.
Homer, Odyssey 13.429-438.
Homer, Odyssey 16.172-176 (the disguise lifted).

title: Raven's Rock and the spring Arethusa
greek: πὰρ Κόρακος πέτρῃ ἐπί τε κρήνῃ Ἀρεθούσῃ (par Korakos petrēi epi te krēnēi Arethousēi)
short: Landmarks near Eumaeus' pig-farm: a rock named after a raven (korax) and a spring called Arethusa.
body: Korax is the ordinary Greek word for a raven (LSJ), so the place is 'Raven's Rock'. Arethusa was a common name for springs; LSJ lists this Ithacan one and the famous spring at Syracuse, which Ovid connects with the myth of a nymph pursued under the sea by the river Alpheus (Metamorphoses 5.572-641). The swine feed on acorns and drink the 'black' (deep, shaded) water, food that Athena says makes them fat. Local tradition on Ithaca places the spring and the cliff in the south-east of the island, but such identifications are modern and uncertain. The landmarks matter for the plot because they show that Eumaeus' farm is far from the town and the palace, a safe place for Odysseus to hide and for Telemachus to land secretly.

Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. Ἀρέθουσα.

anchor: that he might win good report
title: Telemachus' journey for fame (kleos)
greek: ἵνα κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἄροιτο (hina kleos esthlon aroito)
short: Athena explains that she sent Telemachus to Sparta so that he might win a good name for himself.
body: Odysseus asks why Athena did not simply tell his son the truth instead of letting him wander and risk death. Her reply is that the journey was designed to give Telemachus kleos, the report that others give of a man and the root of epic fame. She said the same in Book 1, when she planned the journey 'that he may win good report among men' (1.95). In the second half of the poem the young man's growth into a capable adult, able to act beside his father, depends on his having travelled, been received by kings and survived an ambush. Athena reveals that the suitors are lying in wait with a black ship (13.425-8, cf. 4.842-7), but predicts their failure, setting up the suspense of Telemachus' return in Book 15.

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 1.93-95 (Athena's plan for Telemachus' kleos).
Homer, Odyssey 4.842-847 (the suitors' ambush).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. κλέος.
